page3_img_1.png.title: Mail senders and patch submitters vs. tenure (Postgres)
page3_img_1.png.description: Bar histogram (Postgres) showing counts of active non-developer mailing‑list participants (blue) and active patch submitters (red) by tenure in months (x‑axis). The y‑axis is logarithmic, so the large initial counts (several hundred mail senders and up to a few hundred patch submitters in month 0–1) decline multiplicatively over time. Mail activity (blue) falls steadily but persists out toward ~100 months, whereas patch submitters (red) fall much faster and are largely absent after about 40 months, illustrating the paper’s point that technical engagement (patching) decays much sooner than general mailing‑list participation.

page4_img_1.png.title: Three-panel plots of Apache activity vs. tenure
page4_img_1.png.description: Three adjacent bar charts for the Apache project plotting number of active people (y-axis) against tenure in 30‑day epochs (x-axis). Left: non-developer mailing‑list activity shows a very large initial cohort (a peak ~2,000 people at the first epoch) that falls steeply in the first months and then declines toward zero by ~100 epochs. Middle: developer mailing‑list activity starts much lower (≈50–60 active people early on) and decays gradually over roughly 120 epochs. Right: active committers (file‑commit activity) likewise begin near ≈60 at the start of developer tenure and decrease steadily to single digits by about 50–70 epochs. Together the panels show that mailing‑list participation and committing both decline with tenure, with the non‑developer pool shrinking far more rapidly than the smaller, longer‑lived developer/committer core.

page8_img_1.png.title: LR χ² improvements from adding predictors (Apache, Postgres, Python)
page8_img_1.png.description: The table reports likelihood-ratio χ² improvements when adding predictors to the piecewise hazard models for each project. Adding sent_cum and patches_submitted (two degrees of freedom) yields χ² = 144 for Apache, 62 for Postgres, and 52 for Python, indicating a very large model improvement for Apache and moderate improvements for Postgres and Python. Adding norm_indegree (one degree of freedom) yields χ² = 10 for Apache, 56 for Postgres, and 30 for Python, showing that indegree substantially improves the Postgres model, less so for Python, and only marginally for Apache. These values imply that activity/patch behavior drives fit most strongly in Apache, whereas Postgres benefits roughly equally from activity and social-response measures.

page4_img_2.png.title: Average in-degree of non-developers by mailing-list tenure (months)
page4_img_2.png.description: Bar chart of average in-degree per tenure month (x-axis: tenure in months 0–100; y-axis: "Average indegree for period", ~0.008–0.045) for non-developers. A smoothed grey trend line shows an early rise in in-degree during the first ~10–20 months (from ~0.01 to ~0.018–0.02), a plateau through roughly 40 months, and then a gradual decline toward ~0.01–0.015 by ~60 months. After ~60 months the per-month bars become noisy with several large spikes (up to ~0.04), which the paper notes are unstable because very few participants remain that long (fewer than ~10), so the early-rise/flatten-then-decline pattern is the reliable signal. This pattern supports the paper's claim that non-developers' social visibility (indegree) increases in the first years of tenure, peaks in the second–third year, then decreases as long-tenured non-developers become less active.

page7_img_1.png.title: Postgres smoothed hazard rate of immigration vs. tenure (years)
page7_img_1.png.description: Smoothed hazard function (Postgres) plotting the instantaneous rate at which mailing‑list participants become developers (y‑axis) against tenure in years (x‑axis, 0–5). The curve rises from near 0.001 at entry to a peak of about 0.002–0.0025 around year 1, then falls steadily, reaching roughly 0.0005 by year 5. A small secondary bump appears near year 3 before the continued decline. This non‑monotonic shape (early rise, peak ~1 year, then decline) visually supports the paper’s finding that immigration rates in Postgres increase early in tenure and then decrease over longer tenures.

page7_img_2.png.title: Univariate statistics of predictors for Postgres, Apache, and Python
page7_img_2.png.description: Table 1 reports monthly univariate summary statistics for the predictor variables used in the hazard models, with n = number of monthly records, c = number of distinct non-developer candidates, and i = number who ultimately immigrated. For Postgres (n=178,510; c=3,545; i=20) the mean patches_sub is 0.010 (SD 0.42, max 90), norm_indegree 0.0013 (SD 0.0082, max 0.31), devs_cum 15.70 (SD 4.21, range 1–21), and sent_cum mean 13.52 (SD 67.76, max 2,724). For Apache (n=50,170; c=1,445; i=30) patches_sub mean 0.036 (SD 0.78, max 58), norm_indegree 0.0015 (SD 0.0088, max 0.238), sent_cum mean 7.34 (SD 18.18, max 273), and devs_cum 46.32 (SD 9.76, range 3–57). For Python (n=45,216; c=1,320; i=62) patches_sub mean 0.0072 (SD 0.31, max 46), norm_indegree 0.0039 (SD 0.023, max 1), devs_cum 58.69 (SD 14.21, range 0–79), and sent_cum mean 13.88 (SD 54.45, max 1,648). The table shows highly skewed distributions (means much smaller than maxima and large SDs), indicating that most person-months have zero or very few patches/messages while a small number of participants are extremely active.

page9_img_1.png.title: Hazard-model coefficients for immigration (Apache, Postgres, Python)
page9_img_1.png.description: This table reports the piecewise‑constant proportional hazard model coefficients (log‑proportional effects), z‑scores, and P>|Z| values for three projects (columns: Apache, Postgres, Python). Rows include six tenure periods (tp1–tp6), a normalized in‑degree social measure (norm_indegree), patch submissions (patches_sub), cumulative messages sent (sent_cum), cumulative number of developers (devs_cum), and calendar time trend (time_trend). Key findings shown: norm_indegree is large and highly significant in all three projects (coeffs 54.68, 69.37, 8.54; p≤0.002), patch submission significantly increases hazard in Postgres (0.054, p=0.041) and especially Python (0.093, p<0.001) but is not significant in Apache (0.053, p=0.108), and sent_cum is significant in all models (e.g., Apache 0.021, p<0.001). The time‑period terms (tp1–tp6) are statistically significant in Apache and Postgres (p-values ≤0.034), but not in Python (all p>0.29), and time_trend is negative and significant in Postgres and Python (−2.26, p=0.013; −1.36, p=0.002) while devs_cum shows a positive, significant effect in Postgres and Python but not in Apache.
